narrative:
The model estimated a 96.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and your application was denied because that estimate is very high. This is not a guarantee of failure, but it means the model found your profile much closer to students who did not pass than to those who did.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile. You are in the lowest decile, while accepted students average around the middle of their class. That low standing pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score: 26, compared with an average of about 37 among accepted students. This also pushed toward failure. The third factor was your first-year class-rank decile, again the lowest decile versus an accepted average near the middle, adding further risk. Your undergraduate GPA, family-income bracket, and full-time status were less important in this prediction.

To improve your chances, focus on the areas the model weighted most: prepare to retake the LSAT and seek structured admissions advising. Ask whether you can discuss extenuating circumstances, consider schools with more holistic review, and reapply only after showing stronger academic or test evidence.
